text: Madam Chief Justice may please the court, there is one distinct injury to justice, more reconstruction didn't get paid it's change orders that is established by its pleadings that is established by the testimony of trial that is even established by the statements that are made in the appellee's own briefing. And if I could sort of start well segue into that in just a moment, Madam Chief Justice. I understand in our brief issues one and two are conjoined right because they both relate to this significant and groundbreaking appellee appellant argument about the new interpretation of the one satisfaction doctrine. But I would like first just to talk about very briefly our first issue. Mr Patel was not sued for breach of contract. Mr Patel was not found liable for breach of contract. There were no claims against Mr Patel for breach of contract, tried by consent. There's a judgment right now against Mr Patel jointly and separately with the RCC for breach of contract rule 301 and the Texas state specifically, you can't get a judgment against someone who you didn't sue, who doesn't appear in your pleadings and it is not supported by a jury question or a jury finding that is fundamental error by the trial court, and we're asking this court to correct it by reforming the judgment to only show a breach of contract finding against ERCC for the amounts found by the jury. Going into our second issue and this will talk in more detail about the injuries that were suffered potentially in this case, Madam Chief Justice. The definition of the word unconventional is quote, not based upon what is generally done or believe the appellee admits that they are asking this court to accept something unconventional. I would submit that that is an understatement, if I have ever heard one. What we are arguing for is a whole new legal world that would affect every single civil case in this district by changing our fundamental understanding of the one satisfaction doctrine. That's not hyperbole, justices, and this new standard or interpretation of the law is contained on page 25 of their appellee brief, where they claim that they can recover on multiple theories against multiple defendants, even on a single injury, justices. Because the one satisfaction doctrine, quote, does not apply to reduce recovery when the plaintiff seeks an amount equal to not greater than the amount of its injuries. This court's opinions in Nguyen, in Crowbar Drilling, in Sam Houston v. Sheevak, in Satan, in TMRJ Holdings, all hold that a party that seeks damages under two or more theories for a single injury must, before judgment is rendered, elect which remedy they want the court to render judgment for. These opinions reflect and reference the Supreme Court's opinions in Skyview, in Boyce-Ironworks, in Tony Golo v. Chapa, in Stuart Title, which all say the exact same thing. And these cases also hold that it doesn't matter whether multiple defendants commit multiple different acts, as long as the injury is the same. The Lundy case holds it doesn't even matter if the jury awards different amounts of damages on different causes of action, as long as the injury is the same. And as this court in the 2018 TMRJ case said, it also doesn't even matter if you're seeking monetary and non-monetary relief. If you suffered a single injury, you have a single remedy.

speaker: sherryradack
text: So what's the single injury?

speaker: kevinmadden
text: The single injury here is, Warwick Construction did work, but they didn't get paid for it. Specifically, they didn't get paid about $870,000 in change orders. That is the specific injury, Chief Justice. And nowhere in any of these cases that I've just referenced does this Grand Canyon-sized exception, argued by the appellee, appear anywhere. So there are two alternatives. Either this court and the Texas Supreme Court have simply neglected to memorialize this huge exception to the one satisfactory doctrine, which would eat the rule, by the way, or it's not the law. And it's not the law. And related to your specific question on the how many injuries that there are, in Exhibit 2 to our brief today, we provided the live pleading in this case. We're on page 263. Warwick Construction's sole fraud claim against my clients was that they defrauded us, defrauded Warwick, by making misrepresentations related to a bond. We said we would get a bond, we didn't get it. And as a result of that, when they didn't get paid, there was no bond to make sure that they got paid.

That is implicit not only in the pleadings, in the disclosure responses, but also in the testimony of Mr. Ann and the owner of Warwick Construction. In Exhibit 8, on pages 110 through 112, I specifically asked Mr. Ann about all of his fraud allegations. And he again references only the bond and agrees that this was his misrepresentation allegation in the case. He also stated that the damages related to the misrepresentation were the unpaid change orders. The exact same damage that we were talking about in breach of contract and we're talking about in the Texas Trust Fund Act. So why didn't ERCC pay Warwick for the change orders? And what this case has said, in the Wynn case and multiple other cases, is if you don't elect your remedy, and the trial court doesn't elect your remedy, this court will elect your remedy for you. And in order to attempt to recover where they can't recover, they are asking this court to accept this extraordinary new version of the One Satisfaction Doctrine, which is directly contrary to every opinion that this court has issued in the past 20 years related to that doctrine. I see my time has expired unless the panel has additional questions.

text: Did he have a duty to disclose the joint ownership?

speaker: kevinmadden
text: Thank you, Chief Justice. If I may, just to touch on a couple things that the panel asked and what Ms. Norman answered. She admits, Apelli admits, there was no bonding contractual requirement to obtain a bond between ERCC and Warwick. They referenced the fact of an upstream contract between ERCC and Altus that they were somehow relying upon. It's in our briefing, Justices, I asked at trial Mr. Annan if he was even aware of that contract. He said he was not. I asked him if he could have relied upon that contract in determining whether a bond should have been taken out. He said he couldn't have because he was unaware of its existence. That, I think, resolves the issue about whether there was ever any contractual right or any fraud related to this bond. In terms of whether there's any evidence in the record of all of these other fraudulent things that they talked about, when they're talking about, you know, we have damage with our relationship with our subcontractors, and we're incurring additional costs related to paying people, they put no evidence on the record of that. And when I object, when they talk about the 352, Apelli's counsel says to the judge again, we're only seeking damages related to these change orders, even in terms of the fraud. And the jury can put whatever they want in terms of the damages related to the change orders, but it is the same injury. The fraud is not the injury. The failure to get paid is the injury on fraud, breach of contract, and the Texas Crest Fund Act. In terms of the duty that would potentially arise on non-disclosure, once again, ask Mr. Annan whether ERCC or Mr. Patel or anybody else ever withheld from him any information related to this common ownership. He said they didn't. I asked him whether he ever asked about it. He said he never did. These are red herrings designed to get away from the fact that this is a single injury. And in terms of this $352,000, I'll read from the record, which is part of what our exhibit's in the case. My examination with Mr. Annan, you are not alleging or no longer alleging any fraud related to the 352, correct? His answer, correct. The 352 is we reduce our contract price because you're going to do project management. You didn't do project management. Therefore, fraud has been committed. They waive it specifically at the time of trial. It appears, again, they don't ask for it. Also, when Ms. Norman is arguing before the jury as to the damages that she's wanting, she mentions nothing about this 352. She mentions nothing about damages related to these lack of project management fees. It's only justices, when they get $33,000 from the jury, not the $800,000 that they wanted, that this gets resuscitated in their appellee brief because it has to. Because now they have to figure some way to be able to collect against multiple causes of action. If they had gotten $800,000 on their fraud claim, we would be here before you right now on one or two issues because they would have elected to recover on the fraud. But instead, because they didn't get that, justices, they have to create this new Frankenstein's monster in the one satisfactory doctrine. They have to misstate the record as exactly what happened in terms of the fraud allegations in order to somehow distinguish these injuries. Again, the injury isn't that their contract was breached or that the trust fund was violated or that fraud was committed. The injury is we didn't get paid our money. And that is the injury that in all of the cases from this court and the Texas Supreme Court that talks about the one satisfactory doctrine, that's what you look at. Not all of these different allegations, not what everybody's claiming, but what the central injury is. And the central injury here is nonpayment. I'd say again that my time is expiring, Chief Justice, and unless the court has any additional questions, I'll conclude.
